`GICHighDimension` selects variables in high-dimensional regression by
maximizing a generalized information criterion (GIC). The search is a
Hopfield-network style coordinate search: it visits the candidate variables in
random order, proposes adding a variable that is out of the model or removing
one that is in it, and keeps the move when the criterion improves. The method
is described in Xiao and Walker (2026), *Statistics and Computing*,
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-026-10853-5>.

## Setting up Julia

The search runs in 'Julia' (≥ 1.9). Install Julia from
<https://julialang.org/downloads/>, then connect R to it:

```{r}
library(GICHighDimension)
setup_julia()               # or setup_julia("/path/to/julia/bin")
install_julia_packages()    # first time only
```

## Selecting variables

Simulate a sparse linear model with 30 candidate predictors, 3 of them active:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 300; p <- 30
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
beta <- c(2, -1.5, 1, rep(0, p - 3))
Y <- LP_to_Y(X, beta, family = "Normal")
```

Run the search with EBIC, starting from the first five variables:

```{r}
fit <- GICSelection(
  X, Y,
  Initial_Column      = 1:5,
  Calculate_GIC       = "Calculate_EBIC",
  Calculate_GIC_short = "Calculate_EBIC_short",
  k    = 15,     # skip models with 15 or more variables
  Nsim = 3       # passes over the variables
)

sort(fit$selected_coeffs[[length(fit$selected_coeffs)]])
#> [1] 1 2 3
```

`fit$GIC_values` records the criterion after each of the `Nsim * p` steps, so
`plot(fit$GIC_values, type = "l")` shows the search converging. Models never
have more than `min(k, n) - 1` variables.

## Choosing a criterion

Every criterion has the form
$$
\mathrm{GIC} = \frac{Y^\top H Y}{n} - \frac{K\,\hat\sigma^2}{n}\,c_n ,
$$
where $H$ is the hat matrix of the selected columns, $K$ the number of selected
variables, $\hat\sigma^2$ the residual variance, and $c_n$ the penalty:

| Function | Criterion | Penalty $c_n$ | Reference |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `Calculate_AIC` | AIC | $1$ | Akaike (1974) |
| `Calculate_BIC` | BIC | $\log n$ | Schwarz (1978) |
| `Calculate_CAIC` | Consistent AIC | $1 + \log n$ | Bozdogan (1987) |
| `Calculate_SIC` | Square-root IC | $\sqrt n$ | Shao (1997) |
| `Calculate_GIC2` | GIC$_2$ | $P^{1/3}$ | Kim, Kwon and Choi (2012) |
| `Calculate_GIC3` | GIC$_3$ | $2 \log P$ | Kim, Kwon and Choi (2012) |
| `Calculate_GIC4` | GIC$_4$ | $2(\log P + \log\log P)$ | Kim, Kwon and Choi (2012) |
| `Calculate_GIC5` | GIC$_5$ | $\log\log n \, \log P$ | Kim, Kwon and Choi (2012) |
| `Calculate_GIC6` | GIC$_6$ | $\log n \, \log P$ | Kim, Kwon and Choi (2012) |
| `Calculate_EBIC` | Extended BIC | $\log n + \gamma \log \binom{P}{K}$, $\gamma = 0.6$ by default | Chen and Chen (2008) |

Here $P$ is the number of candidate variables. Three criteria use slightly
different forms (see `?information_criteria`): `Calculate_AICc`, the
small-sample corrected AIC (Hurvich and Tsai, 1989); `Calculate_CAICF`, the
consistent AIC with Fisher information (Bozdogan, 1987); and
`Calculate_AttIC`, an attention-weighted criterion specific to this package.
Pass the name of a criterion and of its `_short` version to `GICSelection()`.
For EBIC, change $\gamma$ with the `gamma` argument.

## Other response types

For a matrix response (several outcomes sharing the same predictors), pass an
$n \times q$ matrix as `Y`; the criterion is then the trace of a $q \times q$
matrix.

For a non-Gaussian response, transform it to the linear-predictor scale with
`Y_to_LP()` before selecting, and estimate the coefficients of the selected
model with `Beta_estimate()`:

```{r}
y_count <- LP_to_Y(X, beta / 2, family = "Poisson")
fit_pois <- GICSelection(X, Y_to_LP(y_count, family = "Poisson"), 1:5,
                         "Calculate_EBIC", "Calculate_EBIC_short", k = 15, Nsim = 3)
selected <- sort(fit_pois$selected_coeffs[[length(fit_pois$selected_coeffs)]])
Beta_estimate(X[, selected, drop = FALSE], y_count, family = "Poisson")
```

The supported families are Normal, Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Gamma,
Exponential, InverseGaussian, NegativeBinomial, Geometric, MultivariateNormal
and Multinomial.

## References

Akaike, H. (1974). A new look at the statistical model identification.
*IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control*, 19(6), 716–723.
<https://doi.org/10.1109/TAC.1974.1100705>

Bozdogan, H. (1987). Model selection and Akaike's information criterion (AIC):
The general theory and its analytical extensions. *Psychometrika*, 52(3),
345–370. <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294361>

Chen, J. and Chen, Z. (2008). Extended Bayesian information criteria for model
selection with large model spaces. *Biometrika*, 95(3), 759–771.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asn034>

Hurvich, C. M. and Tsai, C.-L. (1989). Regression and time series model
selection in small samples. *Biometrika*, 76(2), 297–307.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/76.2.297>

Kim, Y., Kwon, S. and Choi, H. (2012). Consistent model selection criteria on
high dimensions. *Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 13, 1037–1057.
<https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/kim12a.html>

Schwarz, G. (1978). Estimating the dimension of a model. *The Annals of
Statistics*, 6(2), 461–464. <https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344136>

Shao, J. (1997). An asymptotic theory for linear model selection.
*Statistica Sinica*, 7(2), 221–242.

Xiao, Y. and Walker, S. (2026). Fast variable selection under $\ell_0$
regularization in high-dimensions. *Statistics and Computing*, 36(3), 100.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-026-10853-5>
